column1: # Short lessons for the most common findings: why the finding matters, what
# the fix can break and how to undo it, and how to check that it worked. The
# HTML report shows the lesson under each finding it matches.
# Regexes work as in controls.tsv: POSIX extended, case insensitive, the
# section regex matches the whole section name, the message regex any part of
# the message, and the first matching line wins. One lesson covers a topic,
# not one message. Every field is plain text on one line and none is empty.
# VERIFY is one command, with the expected result after "  # ".
# A lesson is advice that people follow as root. Each one must be checked by a
# person against the software's own documentation before it is merged.

column4: Every Linux host has an account named root, so an attacker already knows half of the login and only needs the password or a stolen key. A root login also does not show which person it was. With root login off, an attacker must first get into a normal account and then get past sudo as well.
column5: If root is the only account you can log in with, this change locks you out. First create a normal user with sudo rights, log in as that user from a second terminal and run 'sudo -v'. Keep the first session open until that works. Undo: set PermitRootLogin back in /etc/ssh/sshd_config and reload sshd, from the console if SSH no longer lets you in.
column6: sshd -T | grep -i '^permitrootlogin'  # run as root; expect: permitrootlogin no

column4: Bots try leaked and common passwords against every SSH server on the internet, all day. One weak or reused password on any account is enough to get in. A key cannot be guessed, and it is never sent to the server, so a fake server cannot steal it.
column5: Without a working key you are locked out. Before the change, install your public key on the host (ssh-copy-id), open a new session and check that it logs in without asking for the account password. Keep the old session open until then. Undo: PasswordAuthentication yes in /etc/ssh/sshd_config and reload sshd.
column6: ssh -o PubkeyAuthentication=no -o PreferredAuthentications=password USER@HOST  # from another machine; expect: Permission denied (publickey)

column4: Updates that someone must install by hand are skipped when that person is busy or away. The days between the release of a fix and its installation are when hosts are attacked, because the fix shows everybody where the bug is. Automatic security updates close that gap without you.
column5: A service can restart at update time, and a new kernel is not in use until the next reboot. The default setup installs security updates only, not every update. Undo: systemctl disable --now unattended-upgrades (or dnf-automatic.timer).
column6: systemctl is-active unattended-upgrades || systemctl is-active dnf-automatic.timer  # expect: active

column4: A security update closes a hole that is now public. Attackers compare the old and the new package to find the bug, and working exploits often appear within days. Most break-ins use a known hole that already had a fix, not a new one.
column5: An update can restart a service or change how it behaves. Read the list first (apt list --upgradable, dnf check-update), make a snapshot or backup on hosts that matter, and update one host before the others. A new kernel needs a reboot. Undo: install the earlier version (apt install PACKAGE=VERSION, dnf history undo last).
column6: anzen --check=packages  # expect: no 'security updates pending' line

column3: A vulnerability that attackers use right now
column4: Most published vulnerabilities are never used in an attack. This one is: it is in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog because real attacks with it were seen. That makes it more urgent than a vulnerability with a higher score that nobody uses.
column5: The fix is an update: a package on the host, a newer image for a container (pull it, then recreate the container), a reboot for the kernel. Keep the old image tag until the new one works. When no fix exists yet, make the software harder to reach: take the service off the internet or stop it. Undo: go back to the earlier package version or image tag.
column6: anzen --check=cve  # expect: the finding is gone, or no longer says ACTIVELY EXPLOITED

column4: Without a firewall, every service that listens on a network address can be reached by everybody who can reach the host. That includes the service you started for a test and forgot, and the one a package turned on by itself. A firewall that drops incoming connections by default makes each open port a decision, not an accident.
column5: A firewall switched on over SSH can cut the session you work in. Add the rule that allows your SSH port first, keep a second session open and test a new login before you close it. Ports published by Docker go around ufw and firewalld rules. Undo: ufw disable (or systemctl stop firewalld), from the console if you are locked out.
column6: anzen --check=network  # expect: a firewall reported as active; then test a new SSH login

column2: open publicly|exposed on public interface|listening on|without a password|without authentication
column3: A database or admin service anyone on the network can reach
column4: Databases and caches such as Redis, MongoDB and Elasticsearch were made for trusted networks, and several accept commands without a password by default. Scanners find an open one within hours. The data is then copied, deleted for ransom, or the service is used to run commands on the host.
column5: A service that listens on 127.0.0.1 only can no longer be used from other machines, or from containers that reach it through the host address. Look at who connects first (ss -tnp). When other machines need it, keep the address, add a firewall rule for those machines only, and turn on authentication. Undo: put the earlier bind line back and restart the service.
column6: ss -tlnp  # expect: the port on 127.0.0.1, not on 0.0.0.0 or *; from another machine 'nc -vz HOST PORT' must fail

column4: The privileged flag turns off almost all isolation: the container sees every device of the host, has every capability and runs without seccomp or AppArmor. Root in that container can mount the host disk and become root on the host. One bug in the application is then a full compromise of the host.
column5: Some containers really need one device or one capability, and they fail without the flag until you give them exactly that (--device, --cap-add). Recreate the container and read its log. Undo: recreate it from the earlier compose file.

column3: Container with the Docker socket or a sensitive host path
column4: Access to the Docker socket is root on the host: whoever can talk to it can start a privileged container with the host disk mounted. A read-only mount of the socket does not help, because the API still accepts every command. Mounts of /, /etc or /proc give a similar way out of the container.
column5: Tools that manage containers (dashboards, updaters, CI runners) stop working without the socket. Two honest options: put a socket proxy in between that allows only the API calls the tool needs, or accept the risk with an expiry date in anzen.accept. Undo: put the mount back and recreate the container.
column6: docker inspect -f '{{range .Mounts}}{{.Source}} {{end}}' NAME  # expect: no docker.sock and no host system path

column4: Root in a container is the same user as root on the host, unless user namespaces or rootless mode are in use. Most known ways to escape from a container need root inside it. As a normal user those fail, and files reached through mounts are protected by their permissions.
column5: Files in volumes that belong to root cannot be read by the new user: change their owner to that user ID first. Ports below 1024 cannot be opened: use a higher port inside the container and map it. Undo: remove the user setting and recreate the container.
column6: docker exec NAME id -u  # expect: a number other than 0

column2: private key|credentials file|\.env file|\.netrc|hardcoded secret|secrets in environment
column3: A secret that others can read
column4: A key or token in a file that other users can read can be taken by any process on the host, for example a web application that was broken into and runs as an unprivileged user. Secrets in scripts, .env files and container settings also end up in backups and stay valid long after you forget them.
column5: A service that runs as another user and reads the file fails after chmod 600: look at the owner first (ls -l) and give the file to that user. A secret that was readable on a shared or exposed host may already be copied: replace it with a new one. Undo: set the earlier mode, which the finding shows.
column6: stat -c '%a %U %n' FILE  # expect: 600 and the user that needs the file

column4: After the expiry date, browsers and other clients refuse the connection. People then learn to click through the warning, which is what an attacker between them and the server needs. A certificate that gets this close to its end usually means automatic renewal stopped working and nobody saw it.
column5: A renewal reloads the web server, a short interruption. Find out why the automatic renewal failed (certbot renew --dry-run; port 80 or the DNS record closed) and do not only renew by hand, or the same finding returns in three months. Undo: the old certificate files stay until they are replaced; keep a copy.
column6: openssl x509 -noout -enddate -in CERT_FILE  # expect: a date well in the future

column4: With NOPASSWD, everything that runs as that user is root at once: a malicious package from npm or pip, a browser exploit, a stolen SSH key. The password prompt is the last step between a compromised user account and the whole host.
column5: Scripts, cron jobs and automation tools that call sudo without a terminal stop working. Find them first and give each one a narrow rule for one command (USER ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/COMMAND). Always edit with visudo, which checks the syntax, and keep a root shell open while you test. Undo: put the line back with visudo.
column6: sudo -k; sudo -n true  # as that user; expect: sudo: a password is required
